## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Define** machine learning (Mitchell's E/T/P formulation) and **contrast** it with explicitly-programmed software. *(Understand)*
- **Classify** real problems by learning paradigm — supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement learning. *(Analyze)*
- **Map** the mathematical foundations — calculus, linear algebra, statistics — to the role each plays in machine learning. *(Understand)*
- **Describe** the machine learning workflow and **locate** where modeling sits within it. *(Understand)*

> **Where this sits:** first lesson of the course · next: **The ML Toolkit & First Model**
> (L02), where you set up the tools and train your first classifier.

## Why This Matters

Biodiversity researchers in Puerto Rico monitor frog populations from thousands of hours
of nighttime field recordings. Telling *Eleutherodactylus coqui* from its mountain cousin
*E. portoricensis* by their calls is easy for a trained ear — and nearly impossible to
write down as `if` rules. What threshold? On which measurement? With how much tolerance?

When you cannot write the rules but you *can* collect labeled examples, you are standing
in machine learning's territory: **let the computer find the rules in the data**.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
You don't teach a child to recognize a mango by handing them a specification ("oblong,
9-15 cm, skin blending green to red..."). You point at mangoes until they get it. Machine
learning is teaching software by pointing at examples.
:::

## What Is Machine Learning?

The plain-language version first:

> Machine learning is the science (and art) of programming computers so they can
> **learn from data**.

Two classic definitions sharpen it:

- *"The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being
  explicitly programmed."* — Arthur Samuel, 1959.
- *"A computer program is said to **learn** from experience **E** with respect to some
  task **T** and some performance measure **P**, if its performance on T, as measured
  by P, improves with experience E."* — Tom Mitchell, 1997.

Mitchell's E/T/P version is the one to retain, because it is *checkable*. For the coquí
detector: **T** = label a recording by species, **P** = fraction labeled correctly,
**E** = a set of recordings already labeled by a biologist. If more recordings make the
labels more accurate, the program is learning.

The contrast with traditional programming is the whole point:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph T["Traditional programming"]
    R["Rules (written by you)"] --> P1["Program"]
    D1["Data"] --> P1
    P1 --> A1["Answers"]
  end
  subgraph M["Machine learning"]
    D2["Data"] --> L["Learning algorithm"]
    A2["Answers (labels)"] --> L
    L --> R2["Rules (the model)"]
  end
```

In traditional programming you supply the rules and the data, and the program produces
answers. In machine learning you supply the data *and the answers*, and the algorithm
produces the rules — an artifact we call **the model**. The examples the algorithm
learns from are the **training set**; each example is described by **features**
(measurable properties, like a call's pitch) and, when present, a **label** (the answer,
like the species).

## The Three Learning Paradigms

This course is organized around what kind of feedback the data gives the learner:

| Paradigm | The training data is... | Canonical tasks | Example | In this course |
|----------|----------------------|-----------------|---------|----------------|
| **Supervised learning** | labeled — every example carries the desired answer | classification, regression | species from call features; house price from size | Units II-V |
| **Unsupervised learning** | unlabeled — structure must be found, not matched | clustering, dimensionality reduction | grouping customers by behavior | Units VI-VII |
| **Reinforcement learning** | not a fixed dataset — an *agent* acts and receives rewards | sequential decision making, control | a bot learning a game | Unit VIII (paradigm here; hands-on in the CDAT 4013 lab) |

Two distinctions do most of the classification work for you: **does each example carry
the desired answer** (supervised vs unsupervised), and **does the system act and get
feedback over time** (reinforcement learning).

You will also hear of *semi-supervised*, *self-supervised*, and *transfer* learning —
important variants in modern practice (they deal with the scarcity of labels), but out
of this course's scope; we name them so the terms aren't strangers.

## Mathematical Foundations

The syllabus lists calculus, linear algebra, and statistics as Unit I concepts. You do
not need to master them up front — you need to know **what each one buys you**, and
trust that each unit introduces what it uses:

| Area | What it gives machine learning | Where you'll first feel it |
|------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Linear algebra** | data as vectors and matrices; models as transformations of them | everywhere from Unit II — a dataset *is* a matrix (rows = examples, columns = features) |
| **Calculus** | optimization — following gradients downhill to make a model's error smaller | linear and logistic regression (Unit II); backpropagation (Unit V) |
| **Statistics** | uncertainty — distributions, estimation, and honest evaluation | Naive Bayes and discriminant analysis (Unit II); evaluation metrics (Unit III) |

## The Machine Learning Workflow

Real projects are a loop, not a single call to a magic function. The end-to-end shape
(adapted from Géron's project checklist) recurs in every unit and in your final project:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  F["1 Frame<br/>the problem"] --> G["2 Get<br/>the data"]
  G --> X["3 Explore"]
  X --> P["4 Prepare"]
  P --> M["5 Model"]
  M --> V["6 Evaluate"]
  V --> D["7 Deploy<br/>and monitor"]
  D -.->|"models rot as data drifts"| F
```

Notice where the modeling step sits: it is **one box of seven**. Most working hours go
to framing, data, and evaluation — and the loop closes because deployed models degrade
as the world changes.

| Workflow stage | Where this course develops it |
|----------------|-------------------------------|
| Frame, get, explore, prepare | developed in the labs, as the course needs it |
| Model | Units II (classic), IV (ensembles), V (deep learning), VI-VII (unsupervised) |
| Evaluate | Unit III (the theory of doing this honestly) |
| Deploy and monitor | discussed, not implemented (out of scope) |

## Anchor: Which Paradigm Is It?

The decision procedure in action — five real scenarios, classified:

| Scenario | Labeled answers available? | Acting + rewards? | Verdict |
|----------|---------------------------|-------------------|---------|
| Detect tumors in brain scans, given scans marked by radiologists | yes — the marks | no | supervised (classification) |
| Forecast next year's revenue from past performance metrics | yes — past revenues | no | supervised (regression) |
| Segment customers by purchase behavior, no predefined groups | no | no | unsupervised (clustering) |
| Draw a readable 2-D map of a 300-feature dataset | no | no | unsupervised (dimensionality reduction) |
| Teach a bot to win a game by playing it | not as a dataset | yes — win/lose | reinforcement learning |

Read each verdict back through the two distinctions: labels present? agent acting? That
is the entire skill — and quiz material.

## Discussion

Classify each scenario by paradigm (and task, where it applies). Think alone, then
compare with a neighbor, then we resolve together:

1. Flag fraudulent credit-card transactions, given last year's transactions marked
   fraud / legitimate by investigators.
2. Group the noise sources in Humacao nighttime recordings — coquí, insects, traffic,
   rain — *without* any labeled archive to start from.
3. Tune the timing of traffic lights around the UPR-Humacao entrance to minimize
   average wait, learning from measured delays after each adjustment.

One of these is genuinely arguable — be ready to defend which, and why.

## Deep Dive: Sixty Years in Six Paragraphs (Optional)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="A brief history of machine learning"}

**1950s-60s.** Turing asks whether machines can learn from experience; Samuel's
checkers player improves by playing itself; the perceptron is built as *hardware* to
recognize simple patterns — neural networks are born early.

**1970s-80s.** AI bets on rule-based *expert systems* — human knowledge hand-coded as
rules. They struggle to scale and generalize (the lesson that motivates this whole
course). Backpropagation, popularized in 1986, revives multi-layer neural networks.

**1990s.** Support vector machines and decision trees outperform the era's neural
networks, which suffer from vanishing gradients and overfitting.

**2000s.** The web makes data abundant, and data — not just algorithms — becomes the
key ingredient. Spam filters (Naive Bayes) become ML's first ubiquitous commercial win.

**2010s.** Computational power plus training breakthroughs ignite deep learning:
convolutional networks transform vision, recurrent networks transform speech; AlphaGo
(2016) marries deep learning with reinforcement learning to beat the world Go champion.

**2018 onward.** Transformer architectures revolutionize language processing, leading
to today's conversational systems — built on the same supervised / self-supervised /
reinforcement foundations this course teaches.

:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Are AI, machine learning, and deep learning the same thing?"** — Nested, not equal.
AI is the broad goal (machines doing tasks that need intelligence), machine learning is
the data-driven approach to it, and deep learning is the neural-network branch of
machine learning (Unit V). Most of what makes headlines as "AI" today is ML.

**"Is ML always better than hand-written rules?"** — No. When the logic is known,
simple, and must be auditable (tax brackets, eligibility rules), write the rules. ML
earns its complexity when rules are unknown, fuzzy, or drift over time — and it costs
you data collection, evaluation discipline, and maintenance (the workflow loop above).

**"Do I need to master all that math before I can start?"** — No. The foundations table
is a map, not a gate: your statistics prerequisite plus programming experience are enough
to begin, and each unit introduces the math it actually uses, when it uses it.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Machine learning | programs that improve at a task with experience (data) |
| Model | the rules the algorithm learned; features in, prediction out |
| Training set | the labeled (or unlabeled) examples learned from |
| Supervised | data carries the answers; classify or regress |
| Unsupervised | no answers; find structure (clusters, low-dim maps) |
| Reinforcement | an agent learns a policy from rewards |
| Workflow | frame · data · explore · prepare · model · evaluate · deploy — a loop |
